sections.h2: A large city with very different neighborhoods
sections.html:
Chesapeake is an independent city in Hampton Roads and the second largest city in Virginia by land area. It spans about 351 square miles, roughly 338 of them land. Residents numbered 249,422 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 255,332, which also ranks it second in the state for population.

A lot of that land is protected farmland, forest and wetland, including part of the Great Dismal Swamp National Wildlife Refuge, so one address might be on a dense street near Norfolk and another on a rural road near the North Carolina line. Buyers who know Great Bridge may know little about Deep Creek or Western Branch. The old communities of South Norfolk, Butts Road, Deep Creek, Pleasant Grove, Western Branch and Washington each have their own character, and the same repair problem can be read differently in each.

sections.h2: Housing age and what it means for repairs
sections.html:
The city came together in 1963 when South Norfolk and the rest of Norfolk County consolidated. For decades much of it was suburban or rural, a bedroom community for Norfolk and Virginia Beach, and growth in the 1990s added roads, schools and water demand. Houses built in different decades therefore carry different systems, lot sizes and repair histories.

Older South Norfolk and Deep Creek homes often have deferred maintenance. Newer subdivisions have their own questions, such as drainage and age of the roof. When we look at a house, the build year and the neighborhood tell us where to start.

sections.h2: Water, flood zones and the crawl space
sections.html:
Summers are hot and humid, winters are mild to cool, and yearly precipitation runs roughly 48 inches. The land sits only about 16 feet above sea level among tidal rivers, canals and swamp. That makes drainage the most common selling problem here: a damp crawl space, standing water after heavy rain, or a lot that floods. Appraisers and buyers look hard at these, and they are a frequent reason a listed house lingers.

  • Check the crawl space for standing water, rot in the floor framing and failed vapor barriers.
  • Look at gutters and grading, and note any sump or French drain that has been added.
  • Ask the city or your insurer about the flood zone before you set a price, because flood status affects what a financed buyer can insure.
  • Record the roof's age. Humid summers and storm winds wear shingles out faster.

Drinking water comes mostly from the Northwest River and is treated with reverse osmosis because the river can run salty. The region also draws from Lake Gaston through a 76 mile pipeline. None of that changes a sale, but it explains why you may hear buyers ask about water quality.

Interstate 64 forms part of the Hampton Roads Beltway through the city, I-464 links to downtown Norfolk and Portsmouth, and I-664 heads toward Newport News. U.S. 13, 17, 58 and 460 cross the city, and State Route 168 includes the Chesapeake Expressway toll road. The city maintains 90 bridges and overpasses, five of them drawbridges that open an estimated 30,000 times a year, so rush hour feels different from one address to the next. Hampton Roads Transit buses run here, and Norfolk International is the nearest commercial airport.

Two Navy sites lie inside the city, Northwest Annex and Naval Auxiliary Landing Field Fentress. Public schools and city government are the biggest employers, and owners transferring out, retiring or settling an estate often sell on a schedule set by a job or a posting.

sections.h2: Real estate tax bills and due dates
sections.html:
Chesapeake assesses at 100 percent of fair market value and bills in four quarterly installments.

InstallmentDue date
FirstSeptember 30
SecondDecember 31
ThirdMarch 31
FourthJune 5

Valuation questions go to the City Real Estate Assessor at 757-382-6235. Tax relief for disabled owners and seniors has a May 15 application deadline, and the city runs separate programs for disabled veterans and surviving spouses. The council sets the rate each year, so look at the city's Local Tax Rates page instead of trusting an old bill.

sections.h2: Taxes and transfer costs at closing
sections.html:
In Virginia, unpaid real estate taxes form a lien that ranks ahead of the others and stays until the taxing authority is paid. Your sales contract decides how the tax is prorated between you and the buyer, meaning who pays for which days.

The seller also normally owes a grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 of the sale price, unless the two sides agree otherwise. The price must appear on the first page of the deed, and the clerk of court collects the tax at recording. A few things to settle early:

  • Get a payoff figure from the Treasurer for any unpaid installment.
  • Confirm in writing who pays the grantor tax and the recording costs.
  • Have the title company check for liens, judgments and unpaid utility charges.
  • If the house is part of an estate, confirm who has authority to sign the deed.

Most Chesapeake sellers who contact us are dealing with the house itself rather than the market. Water damage from low ground, deferred repairs and tenant-occupied properties come up again and again.

  • An inherited house that nobody lives in, with taxes and insurance still due.
  • Rot, mold or moisture that would block standard financing.
  • A military or civilian transfer on a short timeline.
  • A rental with a tenant or a lapsed lease.

A cash purchase takes the property in its present state, so you skip repairs, staging and showings. Sometimes we buy directly, and sometimes we bring in a vetted cash buyer. We tell you which applies when we present an offer, and you can weigh it against a listing.

sections.h2: What to expect from the process
sections.html:
First you send us the address and a description of the house, including anything wrong with it. We review the details and give you an offer in writing. If you accept, a local title company opens the file, searches for liens, and prepares the deed and the settlement statement. The closing date is mostly your call, because no lender underwriting sets the pace. Weeks is a reasonable expectation when title is clean, and estate paperwork or liens add time.

Owners who live elsewhere, including military families who have moved, can finish the sale remotely with signed documents. Before you sign anything, ask the Treasurer about balances, and ask the assessor if you think the valuation is off. Those two calls are free and take a few minutes.

faqs.q: How fast can I sell my house in Chesapeake for cash?
faqs.a: It depends on title and the closing date you choose. With no lender underwriting, the pace depends mostly on how quickly the title company clears the file, which can be a matter of weeks. Liens or estate paperwork add time.

faqs.q: When are Chesapeake real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: Installments are due September 30, December 31, March 31 and June 5. Ask the Treasurer's office for a payoff before closing, since any unpaid balance comes out of the sale proceeds.

faqs.q: Does Virginia charge a tax when I sell a house?
faqs.a: Yes, a grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 of the sale price, normally paid by the seller unless the contract says otherwise. The settlement statement shows the exact amount.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Chesapeake house that is in a flood zone or has water damage?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer can take a house with moisture problems or a poor crawl space, and the offer reflects the repairs. Flood status matters more to a financed buyer's insurance than to a cash buyer.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my assessment in Chesapeake?
faqs.a: Call the City Real Estate Assessor at 757-382-6235. The assessor can explain how the property was valued at 100 percent of fair market value.
